prompt: Match each word to what it is, in McConnell's sense.

pairs.right: A prediction that can be right or wrong
A promise to deliver defined work by a date

prompt: A manager says: 'the estimate is May, because that is when we need it'. What has happened?
hint: Did anything about the work change?

choices.text: Nothing wrong; needs and estimates are the same thing
choices.why: They are separate, and comparing them is the point.

choices.text: A target was renamed an estimate
choices.why: Right. Only the word changed; the work did not.

choices.text: The team estimated the work and May came out
choices.why: Nobody estimated; the date came from the need.

choices.text: A commitment was made by the team
choices.why: The team committed to nothing.

prompt: Why do software estimates go wrong mostly on the short side?

choices.text: Managers add padding
choices.why: Padding would push estimates up, not down.

choices.text: Estimates are always made in hours
choices.why: The unit does not cause the bias.

choices.text: Developers deliberately lie to get work approved
choices.why: The bias is honest, not deliberate.

choices.text: People imagine the plan, without interruptions or delays
choices.why: Right. That is the planning fallacy.

prompt: Which parts does a good estimate have, by the lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: When it was made
choices.why: Yes: the cone narrows with decisions.

choices.text: A single number, so nobody is confused
choices.why: A single number hides the range.

choices.text: A range or a probability
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The assumptions it rests on
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: Clinic onboarding took 18 working days and booking is judged 1.2 times as large. What is the estimate by analogy, in days?
Why does an estimate by analogy beat imagining the work?
hint: What do the past 18 days already contain?

choices.text: It uses the estimate made for the old feature
choices.why: It uses the actual duration, not the old estimate.

choices.text: Analogies never need adjusting
choices.why: They always need adjusting for the differences.

choices.text: Past durations include the surprises
choices.why: Right. Nobody had to imagine the sick day; it happened.

choices.text: It is faster to compute
choices.why: Speed is not why it is more accurate.

prompt: Somebody estimates a new feature by choosing the one past feature that went unusually well. What does the lesson say about it?

choices.text: Compare several, look at the spread
choices.why: Right. Picking the analogy that gives the wanted answer is the commonest error.

choices.text: That is the outside view, done correctly
choices.why: The outside view looks at how similar projects went, not the best one.

choices.text: Analogy only works with one comparison
choices.why: More comparisons make it better.

choices.text: It is fine if the feature was built by the same team
choices.why: The same team can have a lucky project.

prompt: Looking at how similar projects actually went, rather than at how this one will go, is what Kahneman called taking the ___ view.
The team spent 128 working days on 40 screens. What is its rate, in days per screen?
At that rate, how many working days for a feature with 7 screens?
What do function points measure?

choices.text: Size seen by the user
choices.why: Right. Inputs, outputs, inquiries, files and interfaces, countable before any code exists.

choices.text: Lines of code once written
choices.why: That is the size measure behind COCOMO.

choices.text: Hours each developer worked
choices.why: That is effort, not size.

choices.text: Story points per Sprint
choices.why: That is velocity, lesson 10.

prompt: A parametric estimate says 22.4 days. What does the lesson warn about the decimal?

choices.text: Decimals are forbidden in estimates
choices.why: Not a rule; the issue is what the decimal implies.

choices.text: False certainty
choices.why: Right. It suggests certainty the estimate does not have: whether the feature needs seven screens is far less certain than a tenth of a day.

choices.text: It proves the rate is reliable
choices.why: A decimal proves nothing about reliability.

choices.text: It should be rounded up to 23 to be safe
choices.why: Rounding does not fix false precision; a range does.

prompt: What is the PERT mean of a task with O = 3, M = 5, P = 13?
What is the PERT standard deviation of the payment integration, O = 3 and P = 20? Give two decimal places.
Why is the payment integration's PERT mean, 7.83, above its most likely value, 6?

choices.text: The mean ignores the optimistic value
choices.why: The formula includes all three.

choices.text: The most likely value was entered wrongly
choices.why: Nothing suggests an error.

choices.text: A long tail to the right
choices.why: Right. The pessimistic value is much further away than the optimistic, and that tail pulls the mean up.

choices.text: PERT always adds 30%
choices.why: There is no fixed addition; the formula weighs the three values.

prompt: What does the triangular mean do differently from the PERT mean?

choices.text: Gives the optimistic value four times the weight
choices.why: PERT gives the most likely four times; triangular gives none extra.

choices.text: Weights the three figures equally
choices.why: Right. So the pessimistic value pulls harder and the mean is more cautious.

choices.text: Ignores the most likely value
choices.why: It includes it, with the same weight as the others.

choices.text: Is always lower than the PERT mean
choices.why: With a long right tail it is higher.

prompt: Order the four totals for the Agenda team's tasks from smallest to largest.
items: Sum of the most likely values
trap: The sum of the most likely values is the smallest, which is why plans built from it run late.

prompt: The four tasks' variances add up to 12.25. What is the standard deviation of the total, in days?
Why not add the four standard deviations directly?

choices.text: It assumes every task runs long together
choices.why: Right. Independent tasks partly cancel, so variances add, not deviations.

choices.text: Standard deviations cannot be negative
choices.why: True and irrelevant.

choices.text: PERT forbids it in its rules
choices.why: The reason is arithmetic, not a rule.

choices.text: It would give a smaller number
choices.why: It gives a larger one, 6.17.

prompt: If the payment sandbox is down for a week, the payment integration and the end-to-end test both run long. What does this do to the 3.5-day spread?

choices.text: Nothing; PERT handles it
choices.why: PERT's addition assumes independence.

choices.text: The mean falls
choices.why: A shared delay does not lower the mean.

choices.text: The real spread is wider
choices.why: Right. The independence assumption fails, so 3.5 is a floor.

choices.text: The spread shrinks, because the tasks move together
choices.why: Moving together widens the spread of the total.

prompt: Analogy, parametric rate and PERT land within two days of each other. What does the lesson make of that?

choices.text: Proof that one method is enough
choices.why: The agreement is valuable because there were several.

choices.text: A coincidence to ignore
choices.why: Agreement across methods is evidence.

choices.text: A reason to average them and drop the range
choices.why: The range is still what to communicate.

choices.text: Strong evidence for the estimate
choices.why: Right. Independent methods agreeing is the best evidence an estimate can have.

prompt: The director needs booking in 18 days, below the most likely outcome. Which levers does the lesson offer? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Move notifications to a week later
choices.why: Yes: scope.

choices.text: Re-estimate until the number is 18
choices.why: That changes the word, not the work.

choices.text: Start the provider's approval this week
choices.why: Yes: cutting the risk's tail.

choices.text: Split the work so more people help
choices.why: Yes: resources, watching the communication cost.

prompt: The provider's sandbox works on day one. What should the team do with its estimate?

choices.text: Raise it, to keep a buffer
choices.why: The new information lowers the risk.

choices.text: Update it; the range tightens
choices.why: Right. Refusing to update is the failure, not updating.

choices.text: Throw it away and start from zero
choices.why: The rest of it still holds.

choices.text: Keep it; changing it looks unprofessional
choices.why: Updating as information arrives is the professional move.

prompt: What did LibreOffice return for =SUM(E2:E5)+1.04*SQRT(SUM(G2:G5))?
What is SQRT called in a spreadsheet set to Portuguese?

choices.text: RAIZ
choices.why: Right. And SUM is SOMA.

choices.text: SOMA
choices.why: That is SUM.

choices.text: RAIZQ
choices.why: Not the name the lesson gives.

choices.text: SQRT, unchanged
choices.why: Function names change with the language of the installation.

prompt: A team plans a feature from the sum of each person's most likely value. What will usually happen, and why?
hint: Each value sits below its mean.

choices.text: It finishes exactly on time, since each person knows their task
choices.why: Knowing the task does not remove the skew.

choices.text: It finishes early, since most likely values are cautious
choices.why: They are optimistic, not cautious.

choices.text: It runs late, since every value sits below its own task's mean
choices.why: Right. Long right tails add up to days nobody planned.

choices.text: It cannot be predicted at all
choices.why: The direction is predictable: late.

prompt: Estimating your own tasks by imagining how they will go, and so underestimating, is the planning ___.
